extracted.intended_audience: authors/researchers planning or conducting systematic reviews who need to choose where to prospectively register their review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers on where and how to prospectively register a systematic review, comparing features of available registries and alternative options for time-stamped protocol/method disclosure. Helps authors choose a suitable register based on costs, processing time, metadata, and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering the service to prospectively register a systematic review
rubrics_metrics.description: Registers must offer the service to prospectively register a systematic review (defined as entering information about a planned systematic review into a database before starting the review process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline requirement: the register should accept entries prior to commencement and provide a place to record title, authors, planned methods, contact details, and other predefined items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Providing oversight of all registered systematic reviews including a search function
rubrics_metrics.description: Registers should provide oversight of all registered systematic reviews, including a searchable interface so authors can check for existing or ongoing reviews on the same or similar questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The search function is particularly important to reduce unintended duplication and research waste; authors should search bibliographic databases and registries before starting a review. More sophisticated search functions (e.g., MeSH support) are preferable as registration numbers grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing time / turn-around time
rubrics_metrics.description: How long the register takes to process and make a registration record visible (e.g., immediate publication, assessed after registration, promises such as 'no longer than 48 hours', or delays of several months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast turnaround is appreciated by authors but may be associated with fees; slower free services (e.g., PROSPERO) may have long processing times due to eligibility/completeness checks. Consider trade-offs between speed and other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost / fee for registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the registry charges a fee for registration or is free of charge (examples: Research Registry and INPLASY charge fees; PROSPERO, OSF Registries, and protocols.io are free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees can provide faster services but may be problematic for unfunded reviews. Authors should weigh affordability against desired processing speed and services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal assessment of submissions vs immediate/publication-after-submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether submissions are formally checked for eligibility and completeness before being made public, or whether records become visible immediately and are assessed later (or not at all).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal checks (PROSPERO, INPLASY, Research Registry) may improve quality/completeness but increase delays. OSF Registries and protocols.io do not perform formal assessments, enabling immediate posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured mandatory fields and metadata depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and number of mandatory structured fields to be completed on registration (systematic-review-specific registries have 24–28 mandatory fields; OSF offers selectable registration forms or an open-ended registration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured fields promote standardized metadata and comparability; open-ended narrative registrations offer flexibility. The depth of information is often left to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search tools sophistication and usability
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the registry's search interface and tools (e.g., PROSPERO offers many search tools including MeSH; some search functions have been reported as suboptimal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As registrations increase, search functions should approach the sophistication of bibliographic databases to efficiently identify duplicates; authors should evaluate how useful the registry's search actually is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Version tracking capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the registry enables version tracking of registration records so changes to planned methods can be tracked over time (noted: PROSPERO, OSF Registries, protocols.io enable version tracking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Version tracking improves transparency about amendments to methods; authors may prefer registries that explicitly support it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of persistent identifiers (DOIs) for registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the registry provides Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) or other persistent identifiers for registration records (examples: INPLASY, OSF Registries, protocols.io provide DOIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOIs facilitate citation, linking, and discoverability of registration records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of authors' contact details in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the registry displays contact details for the registering authors (three systematic-review-specific registers do; OSF Registries and protocols.io do not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact details enable communication between interested parties (e.g., to avoid duplication), but some platforms choose not to display them publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility criteria for accepting registrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific eligibility rules determining which systematic reviews a registry will accept (example: PROSPERO only accepts reviews that include at least one direct health-related outcome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should check registry-specific eligibility before submitting; some registries are limited to health-related reviews or other scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope openness and access restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the register is universally open to all authors or restricted to reviews performed within certain organizations (the article excludes organization-restricted databases like Cochrane, JBI, AHRQ, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors needing a universally accessible registry should avoid organization-restricted databases; consider whether the registry's scope matches the intended audience and inclusion criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic-review-specific registry vs generic registries
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the register is specific to systematic reviews (PROSPERO, Research Registry, INPLASY) or a generic registry open to any study type (OSF Registries, protocols.io).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic-review-specific registries may offer structured fields tailored to reviews; generic registries may provide broader services (project management, data sharing) and flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for sharing collected data and associated materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the platform offers services to share data collected as part of the systematic review or to host protocol documents (OSF Registries and protocols.io provide data-sharing services; repositories like OSF, Figshare, Zenodo offer time-stamped uploads and DOIs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data sharing or hosting of protocol files is important, choose a registry or repository that supports version-tracked, time-stamped uploads with DOIs and aligns with PRISMA 2020 recommendations (Box 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility, indexing, and discoverability of protocol/registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative visibility of registry records versus peer-reviewed protocol publications or preprints; journal publications are indexed in electronic databases and may have higher visibility than registration records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may prefer peer-reviewed protocol publication for quality assurance and indexing, but registration records provide prospective transparency. Consider combining registration with protocol publication or repository deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing, sustainability, and prioritization policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The registry's funding/business model, long-term sustainability, and any prioritization of submissions (e.g., PROSPERO receives NIHR funding and prioritizes UK registrations; funding discontinuation is a risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consider the risk of funding changes affecting service continuity and whether registries prioritize submissions by jurisdiction or funder when choosing where to register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative prospective transparency options (repositories and preregistration services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other options to prospectively and transparently determine planned methods include open-access data repositories (OSF, Figshare, Zenodo), pre-registration services (AsPredicted), and discipline-specific systems (CAMARADES/SyRF); these may offer time-stamped, version-tracked files and DOIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These alternatives can be used to upload protocols or preregistration templates (e.g., PreregRS) and may be combined with registry records depending on priorities for visibility, DOI issuance, privacy, and sharing preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of duplicate or redundant reviews and the registry's role in mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a registry helps prevent unintended duplication of systematic reviews through discoverability and accessible records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because duplicate systematic reviews are a known problem, authors should rely on registry search functions (and bibliographic database searches) to identify ongoing reviews. The registry's ability to reduce duplication depends on completeness, searchability, and uptake.
